rows.synopsis: Frog and Toad try to resist a batch of yummy cookies.
rows.situation: Toad bakes the best cookies he has ever made, and he and Frog keep needing one very, very last bite. Every willpower scheme leaks: the box gets a string, the string gets untied, the shelf gets a ladder, the outside gets a hole with robins standing by, and the river gets a raft headed for the falls.
rows.coping: The victory is giving the whole batch to the robins, and the honesty keeps going: Frog announces they now have lots and lots of willpower, Toad mutters that Frog can keep it, he is going home to bake a cake. Self-control is hard, trying hard not to do what you really want to do, and the show lets the joke land without pretending otherwise.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: one-more-bite comedy plays 2-4; naming willpower and watching every scheme fail lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'try to resist' is the arc; the script supplies the escalating hide-the-box schemes, the raft finale, and the bake-a-cake punchline.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Toad has baked his greatest cookies ever, which is exactly the problem: neither he nor Frog can stop at one very last bite, or the next one. Willpower, they learn, is trying hard not to do something you really want to do, and it is tested by strings, ladders, holes, helpful robins, and a cookie raft bound for a waterfall. The last idea is the one that works, and the friends end the day cookie-less, willpower-rich, and already planning a cake.

rows.synopsis: Frog finds out Toad has never gotten mail before, so he writes Toad a letter.
rows.situation: Toad's sad time of day is sitting on the porch waiting for mail that never comes, not even on his birthday, because in his whole life no one has ever sent him a letter. Frog hears it and leaves with something he must do, then spends the walk to town telling every neighbor it is Toad's very first letter.
rows.coping: Frog fixes the sad time of day at the source, a first letter that says what a best friend should, mailed by the slowest courier available so the suspense is real (and half given away early). The mailbox overflows with the town's follow-up mail, and Toad's verdict lands on the one that matters: he likes Frog's letter best.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: snail-mail comedy plays 2-4; the sad-time-of-day setup and the being-thought-of payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'writes Toad a letter' is the plot; the script adds the sad-time-of-day frame, the town's first-letter anecdotes, the secret blurted early, and the whole-town avalanche. retagged: 'sad, kind' to 'sad, lonely' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
rows.per_story_synopsis: Every day has a sad time for Toad: porch-sitting, mailbox-watching, and mail that never comes, not even on birthdays. Frog's answer is a letter of his own, written until it is just right, then handed to a snail with instructions for speed that the snail has never possessed. By the time the letter arrives, the whole town has added to the pile, and Toad, holding his first mail ever, sorts through poems, recipes, and coupons to find the one he likes best, from his best friend.

rows.synopsis: Toad's delivery of refreshing ice cream to Frog turns into a melty disaster.
rows.situation: Toad cannot choose from Mink's enormous flavor list, so he orders one scoop of every flavor for Frog and himself, then walks home under the hot sun while the tower melts over his eyes. Covered in sticks, leaves, and drips, he becomes the scary thing everyone is fleeing, including a Frog who cannot fly away because he promised to wait right here.
rows.coping: Toad's confession, I have ruined everything, gets met exactly right: Frog names the kindness behind the accident, you wanted to do something nice for us, and solves the melting with a walk instead of a wait. They eat the ice cream at the stand the moment it is scooped, two chocolate cones, no melting, no waiting, and both are glad the scary thing was Toad.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: melting-cone monster comedy plays 2-4; the ruined-gift guilt and the kindness-behind-the-accident line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'melty disaster' is the midpoint; the script adds the one-of-every-flavor decision, the monster-on-the-path panic, and the eat-it-at-the-stand fix.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Choosing one flavor is impossible for Toad, so he chooses all of them, a towering gift for Frog on a blazing hot day. The walk home goes badly one drip at a time until a cone-covered Toad becomes the monster of the meadow, pursued by everyone he likes. When the truth and the puddle are revealed, Frog does what best friends do, spots the kindness inside the accident, and finds the one fix that beats the sun: ice cream eaten exactly where it is scooped.

rows.synopsis: Frog and Toad go to great lengths to find a lost button.
rows.situation: Toad's favorite jacket loses a button on a walk, and only the exact button will do: the search retraces the whole day, through the sneezy meadow, the dark woods, and the river, turning up buttons that are black, two-holed, small, and square, everything except his. Toad declares they will never find it while Frog refuses to quit.
rows.coping: The answer is anticlimactic and true: the button has been on Toad's floor the whole time. He does the repair properly, returning the found buttons, sewing on his own, then handing Frog the jacket itself with every button sewn extra tight, because you are my favorite friend. The day ends with two friends choosing a walk, buttons intact.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wrong-button comedy plays 2-4; the search-fatigue low and the give-the-jacket apology land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'great lengths' is the engine; the script adds the four wrong-button tests, the whole-world-covered-with-buttons low, and the jacket gift.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A missing button on a favorite jacket sends Frog and Toad back over every step of their day, and every finding is wrong: too black, too few holes, too small, too square. The world, Toad concludes, is covered in buttons, none of them his, and the search ends the way hard days do, at home, where the button has been on the floor all along. What Toad does with the relief is the story: a jacket handed over with its buttons sewn on extra tight, for the friend who never stopped looking.

rows.synopsis: Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him.
rows.situation: The most beautiful first day of spring ever is passing while Toad sleeps straight through it, and Frog is lonely without him. Toad counters every invitation with half past spring, a time that does not exist, and Frog has already proven he is excellent at waiting.
rows.coping: Waiting alone loses to a small forgivable fraud: Frog tears the calendar pages so it reads half past spring, and Toad, convinced, gets up and out. On the walk he works out the truth, it is not really half past spring, and forgives it instantly, it is still very beautiful, and I am glad you got me out of bed.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: bed-pushing and calendar comedy plays 2-4; the loneliness of missing a friend, the trick, and Toad's graceful catch of it land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him' hides the wait-all-day structure, the calendar fraud, and Toad's seeing-through-it ending. retagged: 'lonely, hopeful' to 'lonely, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
rows.per_story_synopsis: Spring arrives in full glory, and Toad greets it from under a blanket, negotiating for half past spring, a time that is not on any clock. Frog waits beautifully, then waits badly, tearing calendar pages to make the impossible time arrive. Out on the meadow, Toad notices the cold, then the calendar, then the truth, and lets him off entirely: it is still very beautiful, and being woken into spring with a friend was worth the trick.

rows.synopsis: To prove they're brave, Frog and Toad set off to climb Mount Gloom.
rows.situation: A story about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog raises the question, are we brave? and the test is the tippy top of Mount Gloom, climbed without an umbrella, on a day of dark caves, glowing yellowish eyes, and rocks that tumble bigger and bigger.
rows.coping: Each scare gets answered the way the book heroes would, together: we are not afraid, mostly truthfully, with the cave and its lonely monster behind them. At the top, brave is confirmed, and the punchline is asking to be brave back at Toad's house, where two friends shelter from the storm they climbed into, feeling very brave together.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: cave-and-rock comedy plays 2-4; the are-we-brave question, pretending-not-afraid, and the sheltering-together ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'to prove they're brave' is the setup; the script adds the story-within-story, the cave monster, and the run-for-dessert retreat.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Frog and Toad read about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog and wonder the obvious: are we brave? The test writes itself, the tippy top of Mount Gloom, no umbrella, in the rain. There are dark caves (one occupied by a monster who mostly wanted company), rocks that tumble bigger and bigger, and wind that is too windy, and the two keep answering it the story way, together, we are not afraid. The summit certifies their bravery just in time for them to run back down and be brave indoors, where the cocoa is.

rows.synopsis: Toad thinks the seeds in his new garden are afraid to grow.
rows.situation: Toad plants his very first seeds and meets the gap between quite soon and now: nothing grows. He shouts instructions underground, decides the seeds are afraid, of the dark, then of the rain, and works through the whole comfort catalogue, firefly night lights, stories in the rain, poetry, silly faces, and a full hootenanny.
rows.coping: Morning brings green: the sprouts are up. Frog floats the gentle correction, maybe they were not afraid, maybe they just needed time to grow, and Toad reframes his waiting as work: he kept them company, read them stories, played them music. A gardener is born, and he is off to find a tuba for the garden.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shouting-at-seeds comedy plays 2-4; the waiting-versus-doing lesson and the reframed hard work land 5-7. emotion drawn from the ratified 18-term list (impatience added 2026-11-11). script_vs_synopsis: 'thinks the seeds are afraid' is Toad's theory; the script supplies the quite-soon confusion, the full care-ritual catalogue, and the time-to-grow reveal.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Toad plants his first garden with total confidence and zero patience, and the seeds respond to neither. Clearly they are afraid: of the dark (firefly disco), of the rain (bedtime stories), of silence (poems, songs, silly faces). When the sprouts finally arrive, so does the quieter truth, the seeds were not scared, they were growing at seed speed. Toad hears it, keeps his version too, and marches off to buy a tuba, because a garden this well cared for deserves music.

rows.synopsis: Frog wants to bake a cake for Toad, even though he doesn't know how.
rows.situation: Rabbit's cake smells wonderful but is for a very special day, Tuesday, and waiting a whole day is impossible. Frog invents Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day and bakes with total confidence and no skill: eggs with shells, milk floods, sugar chaos, while Toad watches, wincing, and finally says the hard thing.
rows.coping: The confession, I do not know how to bake a cake, is met with joy instead of mockery: Toad takes over and does it together, until Frog names the takeover, it cannot be Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day when Toad bakes the cake. Toad makes it right with his own strange, hard, not-very-sweet cake, and Frog calls it the best he has ever had, a cake he will always remember.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shell-egg and lumpy-batter comedy plays 2-4; the kind-failure confession, the taken-over feeling named out loud, and the remembered-cake ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'even though he doesn't know how' is the setup; the script adds the Tuesday obsession, the full baking disaster, and the mutual cake preference swap. retagged: 'embarrassed, kind' to 'embarrassed, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
rows.per_story_synopsis: One whiff of Rabbit's Tuesday cake sends Frog to the kitchen on a mission of love, Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day, though his recipe knowledge ends at the word flour. Shells in the bowl, milk over the rim, sugar everywhere, and a guest of honor trying very hard to be polite. The day gets rescued by honesty in both directions: Frog admits he cannot bake, Toad admits being taken over does not feel like together, and the lumpy cake they share ends up the best either has ever had.

rows.synopsis: Frog and Toad attempt to fly their homemade kite despite some doubting Robins.
rows.situation: A homemade kite, a field of robin critics, and a wind that has to be summoned by licking a finger: the first flights crash, and Toad absorbs the verdict that the kite lacks aerodynamics and might as well be thrown away. Frog keeps prescribing confidence, plus running, waving, and shouting up, kite, up.
rows.coping: The very, very last try works, and the kite's reward is dragging both friends into the sky. The rescue chain grows one neighbor at a time until Frog declares the real decision: the kite goes on its adventure without them, everyone lets go on the count of three, and the pair land on the honest summary, flying it took work, confidence, and running and shouting and jumping, and it was fun. Only a little bit of fun.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: kite-crash and dog-walked-by-kite comedy plays 2-4; the doubters-versus-confidence arc and the letting-go ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'despite some doubting Robins' names the hecklers; the script adds the summon-the-wind bit, the whole-town rescue chain, and the deliberate let-go.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Frog has confidence in the homemade kite, Toad has a face full of meadow, and the robins have notes: too heavy, too many holes, no aerodynamics. After every crash there is one more very, very last try, and the try that works lifts them both clean off the ground. The kite, it turns out, also has confidence, and a whole neighborhood grabs the string before Frog and Toad choose the ending they want, letting go, so the kite can reach the top of the sky on its own.

rows.synopsis: Frog handles being lost differently than Toad.
rows.situation: A walk on the wrong path leaves Frog and Toad lost in the woods. Toad cycles through what to do, what to do, and misses lunch in the forecast, while Gopher asks the perfect unhelpful question: do you not know where you are, or not know where you are going?
rows.coping: Frog does not pretend the feeling away, he re-names the day: explorers. The unusual way turns out to be blueberries tested for safety, a babbling brook, a nap in the grass, and maple seeds spinning, and by dusk Toad thanks him for a pleasant afternoon. The exit line carries the whole lesson: you are never truly lost when you are with a friend.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lost-in-the-woods comedy plays 2-4; the staying-calm attempt, the explorer reframe, and the friend-is-the-answer line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'handles being lost differently' is the contrast; the script adds the two-kinds-of-lost Gopher gag, the explorer conversion, and the never-truly-lost close.
rows.per_story_synopsis: One unfamiliar tree later, Frog and Toad are officially lost, and each is lost in his own way: Toad catastrophizing toward a missed lunch, Frog staying calm with visible effort. Then comes the reframe, explorers do not get lost, they discover, and the woods deliver blueberries, a brook, a grassy nap, and spinning maple seeds. Home finds them by dark, as home does, with Toad refusing a repeat tomorrow and keeping the lovely day anyway, because with a friend you are never truly lost.

rows.synopsis: Toad tries everything to think of a story to tell his sick friend.
rows.situation: Frog is in bed looking quite green, even for a frog, and asks for a made-up story, and Toad has nothing. The hunt goes everywhere: porch pacing, flowerpot searching, pump-splashing, story-shouting, head-standing to shake stories loose, and a full hop-jump-skip-flip routine down the big hill.
rows.coping: Toad returns exhausted and green to find Frog recovered, who retires the request, thanks him for giving it such a good try, and then tells Toad one: the story of a toad who could not think of a story, performed exactly as it just happened, ending with the toad tucked into bed. Failure becomes the story, and being cared for gets returned in kind.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shake-the-stories-loose comedy plays 2-4; the caring-until-you-drop arc and the story-of-the-day-itself land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'tries everything' is the shape; the script adds each specific failed method, the role reversal, and the story-within-the-story ending.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Frog is sick and wants only one thing, a story made up out of Toad's imagination, which turns out to be the one thing in the world Toad cannot find. He walks, searches, pumps, shouts, stands on his head, and tumbles down a hill, and comes home empty, dizzy, and green even for a toad. Frog, feeling better, hands the favor back: a story about a toad who could not think of a story, told gently to the friend asleep in his bed.

rows.synopsis: Toad writes a list of things to do, which blows away in the wind.
rows.situation: Toad's mind is filled with everything he has to do, so on Dragonfly's advice he makes a list, and the list becomes the boss: swimming is not on the list, blueberries are not on the list, and letting Frog cross something off is certainly not on the list. Then the wind takes the paper, and running after it is not on the list either.
rows.coping: Frog runs for the list because he has no list, and when it is gone forever, Toad finds the graceful answer: he cannot remember what else was on it, so the only thing to do is sit and do nothing. The day ends with the last item crossed out, go to sleep, and one list amendment from Frog: say good night.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: list-boss comedy plays 2-4; the rigidity-versus-friendship arc, the lost-list crisis, and the doing-nothing resolution land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'blows away in the wind' is the turn; the script adds the list-gags, the not-on-my-list refusals, and the sit-and-do-nothing ending.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Overwhelmed by a busy day, Toad writes a list and discovers the strange comfort of crossing things off, wake up, make breakfast, go to Frog's house. The list starts ruling the day, blocking swims, blueberries, and even a kind Frog holding a pen. When the wind steals it, the crisis dissolves into the best idea yet: with the list gone, there is nothing to do but sit together and do nothing, then cross off go to sleep and add say good night.

rows.synopsis: Toad buys a pair of new shoes just to be like everyone else.
rows.situation: Mink's brand-new shoes make Toad want to run fast, jump high, and have lots of fun too, so he buys the last pair at Squirrel's shop and forces them on a size too small. He spends the whole walk insisting they are perfectly fine while they squeak, trip him, and finally land Frog in the mud.
rows.coping: The honest moment arrives on a mud bank: I thought I wanted new shoes, but now I just feel silly, and my feet hurt. Frog's gentle logic reframes them, they were new when you left the store, now they are old shoes, and old shoes he does not need. Toad frees his toes, gives the shoes and their laces to Robin, and rediscovers that his own bare feet walk exactly as fast as he wants.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: too-small-shoe comedy plays 2-4; the wanting-what-someone-else-has arc and the I-feel-silly admission land 5-7. vocabulary gap: Toad's opening pull is envy, not on the 18-term list, so tagged embarrassed/disappointed as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'just to be like everyone else' is the motive; the script adds the size-too-small squeeze, the mud fall, and the old-shoes-now reasoning.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Mink has new shoes, everyone wants to see them, and suddenly Toad does too, never mind that toads do not wear shoes. The purchase fits like a mistake, squeaks like one, and costs him a whole morning of pretending. The release is two-part, admitting the shoes were for looking like Mink rather than for walking like Toad, and gifting them onward, before the best discovery of the day: his own bare feet can wiggle, run, and jump just fine.

rows.synopsis: Frog helps Toad give his special jacket a night on the town.
rows.situation: A quiet night in is interrupted by the discovery that Toad's special-occasion jacket has sat alone in the dark of the closet for a very long time. The remedy is a manufactured occasion, a night on the town, for the jacket, that escalates through puddle splashes, a rowboat, a swim, every soup on the menu, and a dance that ends in a rip.
rows.coping: The jacket gets its night, and the wearers get theirs, exhausted. The closing arithmetic is the lesson: it was a special occasion, next time the jacket stays home, and the found slippers turn an ordinary night in into exactly the occasion they wanted. Special things, the story suggests, are allowed out on ordinary nights.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: soup-party and dance comedy plays 2-4; the saving-things-for-someday idea and the quiet-night-in payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the jacket premise is new from the script (no catalog synopsis beyond the title pair); the escalation chain and slippers ending are script evidence.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Frog goes hunting for slippers and finds instead a fancy jacket that has been waiting years in the dark for a special occasion that never comes. The cure is immediate: manufacture one. The town tour for the jacket covers puddles, boat trips, a swim, a table for the finest in acorn through plain soup, and one rip too many on the dance floor. The pair tuck the worn-out jacket and themselves back home, where the slippers turn up at last and a quiet night in is revealed as a special occasion of its own.

rows.synopsis: Frog tells Toad about the adventures Toad missed while he was sleeping in.
rows.situation: Toad asks not to be woken, then wakes at afternoon to a full accounting: a picnic breakfast of his favorite things, eaten alone, a two-seat bicycle ridden solo, river-cooling, duck clouds, free ice cream, scarf knitting, and a stage with a band, every moment ending in I wish I had been awake.
rows.coping: Frog closes the tale with the door left open: now that you are awake we can do all those fun things together, and Toad signs up for tomorrow, asking to please be woken. Missing out gets converted into a next time, and the sleepy toad goes back to bed having learned exactly what sleeping in costs.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: the picnic-and-bicycle retelling plays 2-4; the missed-out ache, the replayed wish list, and the wake-me-tomorrow turn land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the retelling structure, the eaten-picnic and stage-dancing beats, and the wake-me-up ending are script evidence (this story's catalog synopsis was not in the quoted set).
rows.per_story_synopsis: Toad bans morning wake-ups and sleeps clean through a day Frog spends wishing he were there. The catch-up is a story told in gifts Toad never got: breakfast with all his favorites, a tandem bicycle with an empty seat, cloud ducks, vanilla ice cream where he would have chosen chocolate. Each I wish I had been awake lands a little heavier until Frog flips it, everything on that list is still available, together. Toad files the lesson where it counts and requests a wake-up call for tomorrow.

rows.synopsis: Toad throws a party in Frog's honor to celebrate a giant squash.
rows.situation: Frog's garden produces a squash so big that Toad declares a festival in Frog's honor, and the preparations snowball: hayrides, corn in the hole, a shiny festival hat, and an outfit befitting the grower. Then the crowd surges to see the hat on the squash, and the guest of honor is flattened.
rows.coping: Toad owns the disaster, your beautiful squash is ruined and it is all my fault, and Frog meets it with the bigger picture: everyone had a lovely time thanks to you, and squash does not just look amazing, it tastes amazing. The festival ends as a feast, squash for everyone, roasted, in sandwiches, in salad, and one casserole for a best friend.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: squash-festival spectacle plays 2-4; the ruined-surprise guilt and the party-becomes-feast resolution land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'throws a party in Frog's honor' is the frame; the script adds the outfit gag, the crowd-crush catastrophe, and the squashed-squash-for-everyone feast.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Frog grows a monumental squash and Toad grows the party to match, complete with hayrides, cider, and a spiffy outfit for the frog of the hour. The reveal goes wrong in one crowd-surge, the squash hat ceremony flattens the champion vegetable, and Toad stands guilty before the whole town. Frog's answer turns the wreckage into the menu, and the festival closes on a table full of squashed squash, a casserole for a best friend, and all's well that ends in a delicious meal.

rows.synopsis: Frog gets sidetracked while running a last-minute errand on Christmas Eve, causing Toad to wonder about where his friend could be.
rows.situation: On Christmas Eve, Frog leaves on a last-minute errand and does not come back when Toad expects him, and Toad is left alone to wonder where his friend could be.
rows.coping: The synopsis centers the worry rather than the outcome: a friend who is late on the night when being together matters most. The expected resolution, Frog's safe return and the errand's reveal, is the classic shape of this story, but it is not verifiable from the synopsis alone.
